article.articleHeadline: Sewage, pollution, possible bacterial infection linked to fish deaths at Panzath Springs
article.articleSummary: Mass fish mortality at Panzath Springs, Qazigund, Anantnag district, Kashmir, during the first week of June 2026, linked to untreated sewage, waste accumulation and a possible bacterial infection. The Fisheries Department report notes dead Schizothorax fish with white patches and haemorrhagic lesions; internal organs largely normal. Symptoms suggest bacterial infection, possibly Aeromonas spp. or Pseudomonas spp., possibly worsened by a secondary fungal infection; exact cause pending laboratory confirmation and pathogen isolation. Pollution amid anthropogenic pressure, with household sewage discharged into the spring, plus plastic waste, dumped food and washing activities. Immunity likely compromised due to oxygen depletion, stressing fish and enabling disease. Initial treatment with potassium permanganate and benzalkonium chloride; de-weeding and cleaning done. Investigations by SKUAST-Kashmir and NSPAAD, with SKUAST-K Rangil team to visit. Recommendations: laboratory analyses, regulate sewage, restrict waste disposal and washing, periodic water-quality monitoring, and community awareness. Sixth mass mortality in Kashmir in six months.

article.articleHeadline: Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in Ituri, Democratic Republic of the Congo
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak declared in Ituri Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo on 15 May 2026 after laboratory confirmation of Bundibugyo virus (Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense). It is the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC, the second Bundibugyo outbreak there, and the third globally. Bundibugyo historically yields a lower case‑fatality rate (30–50%) than Zaire ebolavirus and has no licensed vaccine or specific therapy. As of 21 May 2026, 82 laboratory-confirmed cases and 7 deaths; 668 suspected cases and 171 deaths under investigation; total 750 confirmed or suspected cases, 178 deaths (crude CFR 23.7%). Six Ituri health zones have confirmed cases: Rwampara (31), Bunia (15), Mongbwalu (14), Nyankunde (11), Bambu (1), Nizi (1); four cases in unspecified zones. Imported cases reported in North Kivu (Katwa 2, Goma 1, Butembo 1) and South Kivu (Miti-Murhesa). Uganda reports two laboratory-confirmed imported cases in Kampala (15–16 May), travel from DRC; one death. Index case: Bunia health worker with acute haemorrhagic syndrome (24 Apr; died 27 Apr). WHO declared PHEIC on 17 May 2026.

article.articleHeadline: Brazil suspends world's first single-dose dengue vaccine after two deaths
article.articleSummary: Brazil suspended temporarily the world's first single-dose dengue vaccine after two deaths, following 501,044 vaccinations from January to May 2026, with over half a million vaccinated this year. Dengue is a mosquito-borne disease; the vaccine was developed publicly in Brazil and approved in November. Of the vaccinated, 3,703 (0.7%) had dengue-like symptoms; 42 had more severe reactions. Three severe cases include a 58-year-old man and a 48-year-old woman who died, plus a 38-year-old woman who required intensive care but was discharged. Health authorities cited insufficient data to confirm a causal link and paused vaccination as a precaution pending further evaluation. Trials involving over 16,000 volunteers across 14 states reported 91.6% efficacy against the most severe form. The two-dose TAK-003 is an alternative; Brazil had more than 6,000 dengue deaths in 2024 (about half of global fatalities), with improvements last year.

article.articleHeadline: Amazon's monkeys have contracted a deadly disease from us
article.articleSummary: HBV infection detected in New World monkeys in the Brazilian Amazon amid deforestation and human encroachment. In a study of 88 primates across 28 species, researchers sampled two human-impacted areas (Rondonia and Mato Grosso) and a remote Japurá River region in Amazonas; HBV was found in 17 of 49 primates in the impacted areas, while none of the 39 from the remote area tested positive. Genotypes matched locally circulating human HBV strains, indicating human-to-primate transmission. HBV is a liver pathogen with substantial human mortality; how it reaches monkeys remains unclear. Possible routes include infant/juvenile pet primates released into the wild and increased urban-forest contact. Implications stress deforestation as a driver of cross-species pathogen introduction; buffer zones and halting deforestation are recommended. It is unclear if HBV causes disease in monkeys or sustained transmission; clinical follow-up in captivity is needed. Paper published in EcoHealth.

article.articleSummary: Hantavirus in Indonesia can cause two major syndromes: Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), which targets the lungs and can lead to fluid buildup, and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), which affects the kidneys. The Ministry of Health cautions the public not to panic, noting hantavirus is a rodent-borne zoonosis known in Indonesia since the 1980s. HFRS can progress to low blood pressure, shock, vascular leakage, and acute kidney failure. Prevention emphasizes cleanliness of homes and surroundings to deter rat infestation.

article.articleSummary: Two protected Atlantic forest zones near Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, yielded 1,714 mosquitoes across 52 species. Of 145 female mosquitoes that had recently fed, blood sources were identified in 24 cases: 18 fed on humans; others fed on six birds, one amphibian, one rodent, and one canid. About 7% of collected mosquitoes carried identifiable blood meals, with sources determined in ~38% of those. Larger studies are needed to better track mixed blood meals and broader implications for outbreaks.

article.articleHeadline: Ernakulam district reports second suspected West Nile death; DMO issues alert
article.articleSummary: West Nile fever alert issued in Ernakulam district after a second suspected death (Kadungallur resident) with an earlier probable West Nile fever death in Paravur this week. The district medical officer warned to prevent mosquito-borne spread. West Nile fever is caused by a flavivirus found in migratory birds and transmitted to humans through Culex mosquitoes; it does not spread between people. Symptoms include fever, high body temperature, neck pain, unusual behavior changes, confusion, drowsiness, semi-consciousness, or loss of consciousness. Severe infection can affect the nervous system, causing encephalitis or meningitis. High-risk groups—elderly, immunocompromised, those with underlying conditions, pregnant women, and children—should take extra precautions. Culex mosquitoes breed in stagnant or polluted water; preventing bites is the most effective protection. Seek immediate medical attention if severe symptoms appear.

article.articleSummary: Brazil suspended the one-dose dengue vaccine developed by the Butantan Institute after two suspected deaths potentially linked to vaccination. From January to May 2026, more than 501,000 people, including many health workers, received the vaccine; 3,703 developed dengue-like symptoms and 42 experienced more severe adverse events. Three serious cases were recorded: a 58-year-old man and a 48-year-old woman died, while a 38-year-old woman was admitted to intensive care and later discharged. Health Minister Alexandre Padilha said there are not yet enough data to prove a causal link, but the vaccination campaign was halted as a precaution. The one-dose vaccine could ease mass vaccination compared with TAK-003, the two-dose WHO-listed alternative given three months apart. Brazil reported over 6,000 dengue deaths in 2024, about half of global dengue deaths, though the situation improved last year.

article.articleSummary: DRC’s Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) Ebola outbreak has spread to Uganda, with 515 confirmed cases and 91 deaths reported in DRC and 19 confirmed cases in Uganda (including two deaths and one probable fatal case) as of Sunday. All Ugandan cases are epidemiologically linked to the DRC outbreak, with evidence of imported infections and secondary transmission among contacts and healthcare workers. WHO risk assessment assigns very high risk for DRC, high risk for Uganda and neighboring countries, and low risk for the rest of Africa and globally. Incubation spans 2–21 days; individuals are not contagious until symptoms appear. On June 5, Africa CDC and WHO launched a joint continental preparedness and response plan seeking $518 million to support Africa-wide efforts.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Child with fever and vomiting mistaken for influenza, progresses to meningitis.
article.articleSummary: Enteroviral meningitis diagnosed in a 13-year-old patient in Hanoi, Vietnam. Presented with fever 38.5°C, headache, and postprandial vomiting initially mistaken for influenza; after IV rehydration, persistent severe temporal and vertex headache, positional aggravation, photophobia, and neck stiffness prompted CSF analysis. Cerebrospinal fluid showed marked leukocytosis with predominance of lymphocytes, and Enterovirus infection was confirmed. Enteroviruses spread via fecal–oral and respiratory routes and circulate mainly in summer and autumn. There is no specific antiviral therapy or vaccine; treatment is supportive—anti-inflammatory therapy, fever control, hydration, and monitoring for raised intracranial pressure. After 5 days of treatment the child was alert, fever and vomiting resolved, headaches subsided, and the child was discharged. Prognosis is generally favorable with early detection, but delayed treatment can lead to complications such as myocarditis, pulmonary edema, or cerebral edema. Prevention focuses on handwashing, safe eating, and cleaning frequently touched surfaces.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola Outbreak: The Race to Develop a New Vaccine Faces Many Obstacles.
article.articleSummary: As of June 9, 2026, the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda faces major vaccine-development hurdles. No vaccine or specific therapy is approved for this Bundibugyo strain, unlike prior Zaire Ebola outbreaks. The World Health Organization is prioritizing two candidate vaccines for clinical testing. The most promising is an rVSV-Bundibugyo single-dose vaccine developed by IAVI, which may require 7–9 months before trial readiness. A second candidate, ChAdOx1-Bundibugyo from the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, could be ready sooner (2–3 months) but still needs additional animal data. Challenges include assessing efficacy during emergencies in conflict zones with displacement, fragile health systems, dispersed cases, short outbreak windows, and funding instability, all complicating rapid development and deployment.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola vs Dengue, Malaria, Viral Fever and COVID: How Doctors Differentiate the Symptoms
article.articleSummary: Published 2026-06-09: Ebola shares early signs with dengue, malaria, viral fever, and COVID, complicating diagnosis. In Bengaluru's KIMS Hospitals, Prof. Dr. S M Fayaz says initial symptoms include very high fever, headache, body/muscle pain, and fatigue. Ebola vs dengue is hard early on because both can bleed and lower platelets; however, Ebola progresses to significant internal bleeding and shock, while dengue may involve capillary leak but less systemic bleeding. Ebola vs COVID: Ebola is not primarily a respiratory illness; COVID tends to affect the lungs with cough, sore throat, and altered taste/smell. Ebola vs malaria: malaria often features fever on a 2-3 day cycle. Laboratory tests, including rapid malaria antigen tests, blood smears, platelet counts, and viral screens, along with travel/exposure history aid differentiation. The public is advised to seek medical help for high fever, unexplained bleeding, extreme weakness, or recent travel exposure.

article.articleHeadline: West Nile fever claims two lives in Ernakulam: Health department's advisory, treatment
article.articleSummary: West Nile fever, caused by the West Nile virus, has claimed two lives in Kerala's Ernakulam district this year. Transmitted mainly by Culex mosquitoes—and also via blood transfusions, organ transplants, and breast milk—casual contact is not a route. About 80% of infections are asymptomatic; when symptoms occur, they typically appear within six days of a bite, per the CDC. Signs include body aches, fever, headache, joint pains, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, muscle weakness, tremors, and neck stiffness; severe infection can cause encephalitis or meningitis. High-risk groups include the elderly, immunocompromised, those with underlying illnesses, pregnant women, and children. Mosquitoes breed in stagnant or polluted water, tyres, and discarded containers. Preventive steps: eliminate breeding sites, prevent water stagnation, cover storage, use nets and screens, wear light clothing, apply repellents, and keep surroundings clean. No antiviral treatment exists; mild cases are managed with rest and fluids; severe cases require hospitalization.

article.articleHeadline: Neues Zecken-Virus erstmals in Österreich nachgewiesen
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: New tick-borne virus detected for the first time in Austria.
article.articleSummary: Alongshan virus (ALSV) has been detected in Austria, suggesting circulation in native tick populations for at least two decades. A Lancet Microbe study analyzed about 3,000 ticks collected in 2024, 2,000 archived ticks from 2005–2018, and around 2,000 patient blood samples, using molecular and serological methods. ALSV is present in Vienna, Lower Austria, Upper Austria, Styria, and Vorarlberg, indicating wide geographic distribution in Austria. In blood samples, the virus was not detected directly; however, two individuals showed high levels of ALSV-specific antibodies, indicating past infections, though infections appear rare. The virus was first described in 2017 in China; Europe has since reported cases in Germany, France, Finland, and Switzerland, with Austria now added. The health impact of European ALSV variants remains unclear. Researchers urge including ALSV in tick-borne pathogen surveillance and considering it in undiagnosed illnesses after tick bites. Participating institutions: Medical University of Vienna, AGES, Bernhard Nocht Institute; further large-scale studies are needed.

article.articleSummary: Kerala, India, reports the first Shigella death in Kozhikode as of 9 June 2026. article.articleHeadline: Neues Virus erstmals in Österreich nachgewiesen | Heute.at
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: New Virus Detected for the First Time in Austria
article.articleSummary: On June 9, 2026, researchers from the MedUni Wien Center for Virology report the first detection of Alongshan virus (ALSV) in Austria, published in The Lancet Microbe. Analyzing about 3,000 ticks collected in 2024, 2,000 archived ticks from 2005–2018, and 2,000 patient blood samples using molecular and serological methods, they show ALSV has circulated in ticks for at least 20 years and is geographically widespread, detected in Vienna, Upper Austria, Lower Austria, Styria, and Vorarlberg. No ALSV was identified in the patient samples, though two individuals had high ALSV-specific antibody levels, indicating prior infection, albeit rare. ALSV, first described in China in 2017 in patients with fever and FSME-like symptoms, has since been reported in several European countries including Germany, Finland, France, and Switzerland, with Austria added. Whether European ALSV variants cause human disease remains unclear; larger studies and inclusion in surveillance and diagnostic workups for tick-borne infections are recommended.

article.articleHeadline: "Fast niemand bleibt aus Sorge vor Ansteckung zu Hause": Wie lebt es sich im Ebola-Land Kongo, Frau Raupp?
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: "Hardly anyone stays at home out of fear of infection": What is it like to live in Ebola-Land Kongo, Ms. Raupp?
article.articleSummary: Judith Raupp has lived in eastern DR Congo's Kongo for 15 years, witnessing Ebola outbreaks including 2019. In Kongo, Ebola is less airborne than Covid, and protection includes distancing and handwashing. Outbreaks originate in villages where wild meat is eaten; meat may be infected. Local tests sometimes failed to identify Bundibugyo virus, delaying outbreak recognition; one suspected death was buried in a different coffin. People who helped fell ill; blame directed at higher powers, traditional healers, or preachers. In Ostkongo, distrust of Kinshasa and state institutions is high after decades of war, with 400 militias and violence against aid workers and UN peacekeepers. Goma has decent hospitals; the media are underfunded, with a move to create a fact-checking unit. Fake news on WhatsApp claims Ebola is an NGO fabrication, fueling hostility toward health facilities.

article.articleHeadline: Vì sao trẻ chảy nước dãi nhiều khi mắc tay chân miệng?
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Why do children drool so much when they have hand, foot, and mouth disease?
article.articleSummary: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a highly contagious infection in children under 5, especially under 3, in Vietnam. It is caused mainly by Enterovirus 71 (EV71) and Coxsackievirus A16. Common symptoms include fever, oral ulcers causing painful swallowing, and vesicular rashes on hands and feet; drooling and poor appetite are frequent due to mouth pain. Transmission occurs via respiratory droplets, direct contact, fecal-oral routes, and contaminated surfaces. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive, focusing on hydration and nutrition. Early medical evaluation is advised to prevent serious complications affecting the nervous, respiratory, or cardiovascular systems. Prevention centers on the 3 clean principles: eat clean, live clean, hands clean; avoid sharing utensils; maintain a clean environment and wash hands with soap before meals and after using the toilet. An EV71 vaccine is licensed in Vietnam, with VNVC expediting vaccination for children.

article.articleSummary: Survivors recount the 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, centered in Beni near the Uganda and Rwanda borders. The episode, the second-largest on record, tallied more than 3,400 cases and over 2,200 deaths, with containment achieved after vaccines were deployed. Persistent skepticism, attacks on health workers, and beliefs of a Western conspiracy hindered early response as communities doubted Ebola's existence and feared reintegration of patients. Health Minister K. Muraleedharan announced rapid response teams, intensified sanitation drives, and immediate water-body and food-outlet inspections to halt transmission. Shigellosis is a contagious intestinal infection spread via fecal-oral routes, causing high fever, severe cramps, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea that may be bloody or mucus-containing. The government has ordered zero-tolerance food safety inspections statewide, with strict checks on unhygienic outlets; concerns include reuse of industrial ice in beverages. Surveillance targets Kozhikode, Wayanad, Alappuzha, Pathanamthitta, with dozens of confirmed/probable cases. In Wayanad, more than 160 students reported GI distress at schools in Sulthan Bathery; two students in a separate school tested positive. Water chlorination is being prioritized, wells/borewells inspected, and hospitals prepared for isolation, ORS, and antibiotics.

article.articleHeadline: Kerala shigella outbreak: All about this highly contagious infection
article.articleSummary: Kerala's shigella outbreak affecting schoolchildren across multiple districts has prompted intensified public health surveillance to curb transmission. Shigella bacteria cause shigellosis, transmitted via faecal-oral routes from contaminated food, water, surfaces or hands, with a very low infectious dose and clustering in schools and crowded settings. Typical symptoms include sudden diarrhoea, fever, abdominal cramps, and an urgent need to pass stools; diarrhoea may be bloody or mucous-filled, risking dehydration. Diagnosis relies on clinical features supported by stool culture (antibiotic susceptibility) and rapid PCR testing during outbreaks. Most cases need supportive care; antibiotics are reserved for severe illness or high-risk patients and should be guided by local resistance patterns due to rising resistance. Complications can include dehydration, seizures, severe enteritis, bloodstream infection, and reactive arthritis, especially in children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals. Preventive measures emphasize handwashing, water, sanitation, food handling, and early case identification with exclusion from schools and food-handling activities.

article.articleHeadline: Zecken übertragen neues Virus in Österreich: ALSV entdeckt
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Ticks transmit a new virus in Austria: ALSV detected.
article.articleSummary: Alongshan virus (ALSV), a tick-borne virus, has been detected in Austria for the first time. Researchers at the Medical University of Vienna’s Center for Virology analyzed ~3,000 Austrian ticks collected in 2024, ~2,000 archived ticks from 2005–2018, and ~2,000 patient blood samples. The Lancet Microbe study found ALSV widely distributed across Austria with detections in Vienna, Upper Austria, Lower Austria, Styria, and Vorarlberg, and evidence that the virus has been established in Central Europe for at least 20 years. Infection in humans appears rare: no ALSV was found in patient samples, though two individuals had high ALSV-specific antibodies, indicating past infection. The human disease impact of European ALSV variants remains unclear, though the original Chinese variant is linked to fever and FSME-like symptoms. ALSV has also been reported in Germany, Finland, France, and Switzerland. Global tick-borne viral diseases are rising, underscoring the need for further study.

article.articleHeadline: Survivors share experiences and lessons from Congo's 2018 Ebola outbreak
article.articleSummary: In Beni, eastern Congo, the current Ebola outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus has 550 confirmed cases, 101 deaths and 19 recoveries as of Sunday. Congo's 2018–2020 outbreak—the second-largest on record—had more than 3,400 cases and over 2,200 deaths and was halted in part by vaccines. Skepticism, attacks on health workers, and misinformation slowed responses in both episodes. Vianney Kambale Kombi recalls beliefs that Ebola was witchcraft or a political conspiracy, hindering reintegration of survivors. Dr. Babah Mutuza Lusungu notes a climate of mistrust between residents, authorities, and partners. Esperance Masinda of UNICEF describes caring for Ebola-affected children; after vaccines helped them recover, stigma toward survivors diminished. Officials warn there is no approved vaccine yet for the current outbreak, raising concerns about response in Beni and nearby Ugandan/Rwandan border areas.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola outbreak in DR Congo, death toll surpasses 101; transmission rate has not slowed, say authorities.
article.articleSummary: As of June 9, 2026, DR Congo reports 550 confirmed Ebola cases and 101 deaths, with transmission not slowing. Eastern Ituri province accounts for over 90% of cases. Health officials warn the true burden may be higher due to delayed confirmation and the absence of an approved vaccine or specific treatment. The outbreak is driven by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, one of six Ebola species (others include Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest, Reston, Bombali). Incubation is 2–21 days; symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain, sore throat, nausea, vomiting, and sometimes rash or bleeding leading to organ failure. Transmission occurs through contact with blood or bodily fluids of the infected or deceased, and via zoonotic spillover from animals such as monkeys, apes, and pigs. article.articleHeadline: West Nile Fever Detected In Kerala Amid Shigella Alert: Symptoms, Prevention Tips
article.articleSummary: West Nile fever detected in Kerala’s Ernakulam district amid a Shigella alert with >90 confirmed Shigella cases and multiple deaths across Wayanad, Kozhikode, Malappuram and Kannur. West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne infection; Shigella is a bacterial enteric disease, and the outbreaks are unrelated. Authorities have intensified mosquito-control, sanitation, surveillance and public awareness during the monsoon. West Nile is transmitted when mosquitoes bite infected birds; humans are dead-end hosts and do not spread it via casual contact. No vaccine or specific antiviral exists; treatment is supportive. Seek urgent care for fever with neurological symptoms; emphasize eliminating stagnant water and safe water, plus hand hygiene.

article.articleHeadline: Programa reduz casos de dengue em 98% com uso de biotecnologia
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Program reduces dengue cases by 98% with the use of biotechnology.
article.articleSummary: Dengue in Águas de São Pedro, a tourist town in inland São Paulo, Brazil, dropped by about 98% in the first four months of 2026, with only 3 cases versus 152 in Jan–Apr 2025. The reduction comes from Aedes do Bem, a biotechnology developed by Flyttr (formerly Oxitec), deployed alongside cleanup drives and awareness campaigns. The program releases non-biting male Aedes aegypti; when they mate with local females, offspring fail to reach adulthood, progressively reducing the population of the dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and yellow fever vector. Initiated in April 2025 via release boxes that act as mini-factories, eggs are activated with water and emerging adults released. The approach has CTNBio biosafety approval and has demonstrated up to 96% efficacy in Frontiers studies. With expansion for another season, Águas de São Pedro joins Brazilian cities adopting biotechnology to supplement traditional vector control.

article.articleSummary: Kerala, India, reports a Shigellosis outbreak with 85 confirmed Shigella infections and over 70 probable cases as of June 7, 2026, according to the Kerala Health Department; one death—a four-year-old child in Kozhikode—has been recorded. Transmission is faecal-oral via contaminated food or water, poor sanitation, inadequate hand hygiene, or direct contact, particularly in crowded settings. Prevention focuses on handwashing with soap and water, safe drinking water, and thorough washing of fruits and vegetables. Seek medical care for persistent fever, bloody stools, severe dehydration, reduced urination, dry mouth, confusion, or other dehydration signs.

article.articleSummary: Jakarta, Indonesia — Pest control is crucial in urban settings like Jakarta, where homes, offices, restaurants, apartments, and hotels host rats, cockroaches, termites, and other pests. Termites do not transmit disease but cause structural damage, economic losses, and higher accident risk due to weakened buildings. Indonesia's hantavirus risk is lower than in several regions of North America and East Asia. article.articleHeadline: Ancaman Zoonosis Bagaimana Perubahan Iklim Memaksa Virus Pindah Rumah ke Manusia
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: The Zoonotic Threat: How Climate Change Is Forcing Viruses to Jump to Humans
article.articleSummary: Climate change drives a pathogen habitat shift, fueling zoonoses across tropical and polar regions. Warming disrupts ecosystems, prompting wildlife migrations and increased encounters with humans, creating spillover risk. Mechanisms include wild animal migration bringing thousands of novel viruses, expansion of vectors like Aedes aegypti mosquitoes enabling malaria, dengue, and Zika in previously cooler areas, and permafrost thaw releasing ancient pathogens into modern environments. Deforestation and agricultural expansion shrink buffers between wildlife and settlements, concentrating interactions with bats, a key natural reservoir for many viruses, including coronaviruses, in farms and urban interfaces. High-risk contact is greatest in biodiversity-rich regions undergoing rapid land-use change, notably Southeast Asia and the Amazon basin. Researchers estimate about 1.6 million undiscovered viruses exist in mammals and birds, with roughly half potentially capable of infecting humans. Mitigation requires integrated human-animal-environment health approaches.

article.articleSummary: Ebola is a zoonotic disease with fruit bats as the natural reservoir; the virus cycles in bat populations, spills over to intermediary hosts such as primates, and then to humans. The index case is often a hunter or animal handler, after which human-to-human transmission propagates, especially within homes and healthcare settings. High-risk groups include those handling sick or dead animals, family caregivers, healthcare and laboratory workers, funeral teams, traditional healers, and religious caregivers; safe and dignified burials by trained teams are essential. Incubation ranges from 2 to 21 days; individuals are only infectious after symptom onset. Early symptoms are non-specific: abrupt fever (38–39°C), fatigue, myalgia, headache, sore throat, with some patients developing a rash. In Bundibugyo Ebola, bleeding is less common than in Zaire or Sudan strains; severe disease features vomiting, diarrhea, and kidney/liver failure. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, about 35% of cases occur among housewives or family caregivers, with healthcare workers affected. Efficient outbreak control relies on community awareness, infection prevention, and thorough exposure history. Published 2026-06-09.

article.articleHeadline: Zeckenvirus Alongshan erstmals in Österreich nachgewiesen
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Alongshan tick-borne virus detected in Austria for the first time.
article.articleSummary: Alongshan virus (ALSV) has been detected in Austria for the first time. In a MedUni Wien study, researchers analyzed about 3,000 ticks collected in 2024, 2,000 archived ticks from 2005–2018, and 2,000 human blood samples using molecular and serological methods. ALSV was found in ticks across Vienna, Lower Austria, Upper Austria, Styria, and Vorarlberg, indicating broad geographic circulation. In human samples, no viral genome was detected, but two individuals showed high ALSV-specific antibody titers, suggesting past infection. Tick-borne viruses pose increasing public-health challenges; established pathogens such as Tick-Borne Encephalitis virus (FSME) and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus cause many infections. ALSV, first described in 2017 in China, has since been detected in several European countries, including Germany, Finland, France, and Switzerland. The clinical relevance of European ALSV variants remains unclear; large studies are needed to determine pathogenicity, prevalence, and disease burden. Surveillance should consider ALSV in post-exposure febrile syndromes.
